analysis.body:
AI adoption in retail trade reached 15.5% according to the Census Bureau's latest Business Time Use Survey, a marginal increase from 15.2% in the prior period, indicating measured but still-limited penetration across the sector. The Census measure tracks firms using AI in the two weeks preceding the survey, providing a consistent baseline as the agency updates this figure fortnightly alongside all other industries.

Retailers deploying AI concentrate on inventory visibility and pricing decisions rather than broader AI infrastructure. IHL Group's 2026 study of 96 specialty retail brands found that inventory data accuracy, not AI budget size, separates winners from laggards, and that most retail AI budgets fund the wrong layer first. Concrete examples show targeted applications: Nature's Emporium uses AI-powered pricing and demand modeling through Retailgrid to inform decisions across supplements and other categories, while Dr. Squatch deployed AI-powered estimated delivery dates and recommendation engines that achieved a 31.89% recommendation click-through rate and attributed $32,978 in Q1 revenue, along with a 25% reduction in customer service inquiries about shipping status.

The economic impact of gaps in AI deployment remains substantial. IHL Group reports that empty shelves cost the retail sector $690.9 billion annually, though inventory distortion overall has declined to $1.7 trillion. These figures underscore why retailers are beginning to move AI from pilot stage to floor operations, even as most budgets remain concentrated in the foundational data and software layers rather than field deployment.

Vendor and market activity centers on supply-chain optimization and customer experience automation. Coresight Research and IHL Group both track AI spending in merchandising and logistics, while case studies document deployments ranging from AI vision for shelf execution to robotics and autonomous vehicles in warehousing environments. The National Retail Federation provides the industry's primary platform for tracking adoption of store automation, computer vision for inventory, and customer-experience software.

For retailers considering AI investment, the data suggests that adoption remains selective and ROI depends heavily on infrastructure readiness. Where results are measured, they tend to cluster around specific, high-impact processes: prescription fill rates improved 20% for a pharmacy-focused operator, delivery accuracy reached 94%, and marketing lift materialized when AI could integrate sales data with competitive pricing. The pattern indicates that successful deployment requires alignment between data quality and tool selection, rather than budget size alone driving outcomes.

https://ihlservices.com/.brief: IHL Group conducts research on retail technology spending and strategy. According to their 2026 study of 96 specialty retail brands, inventory data accuracy rather than AI budget size determines which specialty retailers succeed, and most retail AI budgets fund the wrong infrastructure layer first. The organisation also reports that inventory distortion has declined to $1.7 trillion, though empty shelves still cost $690.9 billion annually. IHL's analysis finds that the presence of AI does not predict pricing-platform quality among vendors, and retailers should instead evaluate explainability, automation controls, and governance safeguards.
